_comment: Authored social copy for the Omarchy showcase packets. Three independently written voices per target, per the social-bundle contract: X and both LinkedIn openers never share a first sentence, no em or en dashes, and NO LINKS OR INSTALL COMMANDS IN THIS FILE. build-showcase-packet.py appends those deterministically from the live catalog, which is what stops a link from ever depending on prose being right.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: Bazaar
targets.angle: The marketplace browser, with the ranking argument as the hook.
targets.x_post:
omarchy's plugin marketplace crossed 1,300 plugins. browsing that in a browser is miserable, so i built the marketplace INTO the omarchy bar.

search every listing, filter by category, hit enter and the install command is on your clipboard.

the part i care about: it ranks by trending, which is views per day since listing. a cumulative install counter only ever rewards being old. something listed tuesday that everyone is copying should beat something from july that peaked in july.

quickshell + qml, no key, no account.

#Omarchy #Hyprland #ArchLinux #Linux
targets.li_personal:
A leaderboard sorted by a cumulative counter is not a leaderboard. It is a seniority list.

That is the thing I kept running into browsing the Omarchy plugin marketplace, which crossed 1,300 listings this month and adds dozens a day. Sort by installs and you get whatever has been listed longest. The plugin twelve people found yesterday and told their friends about is invisible, because it has had one day to accumulate.

So Bazaar ranks by views per day since listing instead. Age stops being an advantage and momentum starts being one.

It runs in the bar. Type to search every listed plugin, filter by category or tag, press enter and the install command is copied. The pill counts what has been listed since the last time you looked and goes quiet when you are current, which is the rule every widget I ship follows: if there is nothing to say, say nothing.

46 tests on the parse path, no key, no account.

#Omarchy #Hyprland #Quickshell #Linux #OpenSource
targets.li_company:
Intent Solutions has released Bazaar, a marketplace browser for the Omarchy desktop that runs inside the system bar.

The design decision worth noting is the ranking model. The Omarchy plugin marketplace passed 1,300 listings this month, and the conventional sort, by cumulative install count, systematically favours whatever was published earliest. Bazaar ranks by views per day since listing, a velocity measure, so recently published work competes on adoption rate rather than on tenure.

The widget carries search across every listed plugin, filtering by category and tag, and one-keystroke copy of an install command. It requires no account and no API key, and the entire parse path is covered by 46 tests that run without a shell.

#Omarchy #DeveloperTools #OpenSource #Linux #Quickshell
targets.posting_note: Bazaar is the highest-view entry in the set and has zero hearts. The heart button is on the listing page, top right. Worth one click while you have it open.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: Pit Wall
targets.angle: F1 on the bar, hook is the widget that knows to shut up.
targets.x_post:
f1 race weekend, live, on the omarchy bar.

countdown to the next session, flips to live timing the second the session starts. leaderboard, gaps, both championships in the panel. free keyless data from jolpica and openf1.

best part is what it does on a tuesday in august. nothing. the slot collapses and you get the bar space back until friday practice.

built on quickshell for omarchy quattro, so it runs on hyprland like everything else on that bar.

#Omarchy #Formula1 #Hyprland #Linux
targets.li_personal:
Most desktop widgets are built by people who never had to look at them on a boring day.

Pit Wall puts the Formula 1 race weekend on the Omarchy bar. Countdown to the next session, then live timing with gaps the moment one starts, plus the weekend schedule in local time and both championship tables in the panel.

The design work that took the longest was the off week. There are 24 race weekends in a season and roughly 340 days that are not one, and a widget that holds bar real estate for a countdown to something eleven days away is a widget you will eventually uninstall. So the slot collapses to nothing between weekends and comes back on its own.

I spent twenty years in operations before I wrote software. The screens that survive on a wall are the ones that stay dark when nothing is happening, because that is what makes you look up when they are not.

Data comes free and keyless from jolpica and openf1, and 30 tests cover the parse path.

#Formula1 #Omarchy #Hyprland #Linux #Quickshell
targets.li_company:
Formula 1 timing now runs natively on the Omarchy desktop bar, through Pit Wall, released by Intent Solutions.

The widget provides a countdown to the next session that transitions automatically to live timing, with running order and gaps, the weekend schedule rendered in the viewer's local time, and both the drivers' and constructors' standings.

The engineering constraint the team set was that the widget must earn its place on the bar on days when there is no racing. It does not: outside a race weekend the slot collapses entirely and returns without user action. That behaviour follows the peripheral display principle that an ambient indicator must be ignorable to remain useful.

All data is sourced free and without credentials from the jolpica and openf1 projects. No account or API key is required.

#Formula1 #Omarchy #Linux #OpenSource #Motorsport
targets.posting_note: Pit Wall has 3 hearts, the most of any entry in the set, and 19 copies. It is the strongest social proof we have. Lead the week with it if you are choosing an order.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: Wait State
targets.angle: PSI. The hook is that every other system monitor measures the wrong thing.
targets.x_post:
new omarchy plugin: your cpu graph cannot tell the difference between working hard and being stuck.

100% cpu compiling is fine. 100% cpu thrashing on swap is your afternoon gone. same graph.

wait state reads linux pressure stall information, the kernel telling you how much time real tasks spent BLOCKED waiting on cpu, memory or io. that is the number you actually wanted. omarchy bar shows the worst current bottleneck, panel keeps six hours.

PSI has been in every kernel since 4.20 and almost nothing on arch surfaces it.

#Omarchy #Linux #ArchLinux #Hyprland
targets.li_personal:
Load average lies to you, and it has been lying since 1993. That is the problem the newest plugin I shipped for Omarchy exists to fix.

Every system monitor on your desktop shows utilisation: how busy the machine is. Almost none show pressure: how much time your actual work spent stopped, waiting on a resource it could not get. Those are different questions, and only the second one explains why the machine feels bad.

The Linux kernel has answered the second one since version 4.20. Pressure stall information reports, per resource, the share of time tasks were stalled on CPU, memory or I/O. It is sitting in /proc on every machine reading this and hardly anything surfaces it.

Wait State puts it on the Omarchy bar. Worst current bottleneck on the pill, short and long pressure windows plus six hours of bounded history in the panel, and plain language for what each signal can and cannot prove.

That last part matters more than the graph. A monitor that overstates what it knows is worse than no monitor, because you will act on it. 26 tests, no network, no key.

#Linux #Performance #Observability #Omarchy #SRE
targets.li_company:
Intent Solutions has released Wait State, a pressure monitoring widget for the Omarchy desktop.

Conventional system monitors report resource utilisation. Utilisation cannot distinguish productive saturation, such as a compile using all available CPU, from a stall, such as a process blocked on memory reclaim. The distinction determines whether intervention is warranted.

Wait State reports pressure stall information, the kernel facility available since Linux 4.20 that measures the proportion of time tasks spent blocked on CPU, memory or I/O. The bar surfaces the current worst bottleneck; the panel carries short and long pressure windows, full stall visibility, and six hours of bounded history.

The panel also states explicitly what each signal can and cannot establish. A monitoring surface that overstates the scope of its evidence produces worse operational decisions than no monitoring at all.

Operates entirely locally with no network access and no credentials.

#Linux #Observability #Performance #Omarchy #OpenSource
targets.posting_note: Wait State has 100 views and zero hearts. Same as Bazaar. Click the heart on the listing page.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: MLB Booth

live mlb on the omarchy bar, and it is not a scraped box score.

it pulls GUMBO, the same feed mlb's own gameday runs on. score, half inning, count, outs, every 20 seconds. panel adds the line score, base state, matchup, last play, the week ahead and the division race.

any of the 30 clubs. free, keyless, no account. quickshell widget, omarchy quattro.

lifelong braves fan, so guess which one i tested against for a month.

#Omarchy #MLB #Hyprland #Linux
targets.li_personal:
If you are going to put live sports on a status bar, get the data from the same place the official app does.

MLB Booth reads GUMBO, the feed that MLB's own Gameday runs on. Not a scrape, not a third party mirror that goes stale in the seventh. Score, half inning, count and outs on the pill every 20 seconds, and the panel carries the line score, base state, the pitcher and batter matchup, the last play, the week's schedule and the division race.

The reason provenance matters here is the same reason it matters in a system I would bill a client for. A number on a display is a claim, and a claim is only as good as where it came from. A scraped score that is two innings behind is not a slightly worse version of a live score. It is a different thing pretending to be the same thing.

Pick any of the 30 clubs. Free, keyless, no account. 49 tests on the parse path.

#MLB #Baseball #Omarchy #Linux #OpenSource
targets.li_company:
MLB Booth, released by Intent Solutions, brings live Major League Baseball to the Omarchy desktop bar.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: X Files
targets.angle: Replies to your own posts. Hook is the spend meter, because everyone else hides the cost.
targets.x_post:
reading the replies to your own posts on X is genuinely bad. the feed buries a good conversation under six hours of unrelated timeline.

so i built an omarchy plugin that pulls them onto the linux desktop instead. classified digests, verbatim quotes, and a queue you drain rather than a feed you scroll.

it costs a few dollars a month in api credits, so there is a spend meter in the omarchy bar pill that changes color at your cap. i am not shipping something that quietly runs up a bill and calling it free.

#Omarchy #Hyprland #Linux #BuildInPublic
targets.li_personal:
Any tool that spends your money on your behalf should show you the meter, permanently, without being asked. That rule shaped X Files, the plugin I shipped this week for the Omarchy Linux desktop.

X Files reads the replies to your own X posts and puts them on the desktop: classified digests per post, volume and velocity, verbatim quotes, and a drainable queue of the ones that actually need an answer from you.

It runs on X API credits, which cost real money, a few dollars a month at normal use. So the running spend is on the pill at all times and the pill changes colour at your configured cap. Not in a settings screen you have to go find. On the bar, next to the count.

I ran restaurants and a trucking authority for twenty years before software, and the fastest way to lose someone's trust is a charge they did not see coming. It is not different because the number is small, and it is not different because the thing is software.

Authentication goes through a separate login helper, so the widget itself never sees your token. 48 tests.

#DeveloperTools #Omarchy #Linux #API #OpenSource
targets.li_company:
Intent Solutions has released X Files, a desktop client for the replies to your own X posts, running on the Omarchy bar.

The widget produces per post digests covering reply volume and velocity with classified buckets and verbatim quotes, alongside a drainable queue of replies requiring a response.

Because the widget consumes metered X API credits, cumulative monthly spend is displayed permanently on the bar and the indicator changes state at a user configured cap. Cost disclosure was treated as a primary interface element rather than a settings page detail: a tool that spends on a user's behalf without continuous disclosure transfers a risk the user never accepted.

Credentials are handled by a separate login helper and are never visible to the widget process. The parse path carries 48 offline tests.

#Omarchy #DeveloperTools #API #Linux #OpenSource
targets.posting_note: X Files has 89 views and 1 copy. It is the newest and the least proven. Do not oversell it, the spend meter angle is the honest hook and it is a good one.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: Docket
targets.angle: PR queue. Hook is the dismissal that expires.
targets.x_post:
github notifications are a feed. what you actually need is a queue. so that is what i put on the omarchy bar.

docket answers one question every 15 minutes with one graphql call: what pull request is waiting on ME. three lanes, oldest obligation first, anything you are late on gets marked.

the bit i am proud of: dismiss a row and the dismissal expires the instant the pr changes. snoozing something is not the same as deciding it does not matter.

81 tests. quickshell, omarchy quattro, token never touches a process argument.

#Omarchy #GitHub #Hyprland #Linux
targets.li_personal:
The difference between a feed and a queue is whether it can ever be empty. That distinction is the entire design of Docket, the newest plugin I have shipped for the Omarchy desktop.

GitHub notifications are a feed. They arrive, they accumulate, and the state you are actually chasing, which pull requests are blocked on me right now, is somewhere inside them. Docket answers only that question. One GraphQL call every 15 minutes, three lanes, oldest obligation first, with a review clock that marks anything you are late on. The pill collapses to nothing when the docket is clear, which is the whole point of a queue.

The design detail I care about most is the dismissal. You can push a row away, and that dismissal expires the moment the pull request changes. Snoozing something is a statement about right now. It is not a statement about a pull request that has since been rewritten, and a tool that treats those as the same thing is training you to ignore it.

81 tests, the most of any widget I have shipped. Authentication goes through a login helper, so your token never lands in a process argument where another user can read it out of proc.

#GitHub #DeveloperTools #Omarchy #CodeReview #Linux
targets.li_company:
Docket, released by Intent Solutions, presents the GitHub pull requests awaiting a specific user's action as a drainable queue on the Omarchy desktop bar.

A single GraphQL query on a 15 minute interval resolves one question: which pull requests are blocked on this user. Results are presented in three lanes ordered by age of obligation, with a review clock marking overdue items. The bar indicator collapses when the queue is empty.

Dismissals are time bounded by state rather than by clock: dismissing an item suppresses it only until the underlying pull request changes. Treating a deferral as permanent across a substantive change is the failure mode that causes users to stop trusting a queue.

Authentication is delegated to a separate login helper so that credentials never appear in a process argument list. The implementation carries 81 offline tests.

#GitHub #DeveloperTools #Omarchy #EngineeringProductivity #OpenSource
targets.posting_note: Docket has the biggest test suite in the set at 81. The security detail about tokens never reaching an argv is real and specific, keep it in.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: Crew Chief
targets.angle: Agent session state. Hook is the blocked agent nobody noticed.
targets.x_post:
run more than two coding agents at once and the expensive failure is not a bad diff. it is one sitting blocked on a yes/no prompt for forty minutes in a terminal you are not looking at.

crew chief puts every running agent session on the omarchy bar. claude code, codex, goose, kilo, pi, whatever. the pill goes loud the moment one needs you or finishes.

panel lists project, harness, state and age, attention first. adapters for claude code and codex plus a one command reporter for anything else.

quickshell widget, arch, hyprland, omarchy quattro.

#Omarchy #AI #Hyprland #Linux
targets.li_personal:
The cost of running several AI coding agents at once is not what people think it is, and it is why Crew Chief now sits on my Omarchy bar.

It is not a bad diff. You review those. It is one agent sitting blocked on a yes or no prompt for forty minutes in a terminal window that is behind three others, while you sit ten feet away assuming it is working.

Crew Chief puts every running agent session on the Omarchy bar. The pill counts them and goes loud the instant one needs your input or finishes its run. The panel lists each session with project, harness, state and age, sorted attention first.

This is a dispatch problem, and I have run one before. Twenty years in multi unit operations and then a six truck authority, and the job is always the same: knowing which unit is stopped, and why, before someone tells you. Agents are the same shape. They just do not call.

Adapters ship for Claude Code and Codex, plus a one command reporter that makes any other harness report in. 23 tests, entirely local, no network.

#AI #DeveloperTools #Omarchy #Agents #Linux
targets.li_company:
Intent Solutions has released Crew Chief, a session monitor for AI coding agents running on the Omarchy desktop bar.

As multi agent workflows become routine, the dominant efficiency loss is not incorrect output but idle time: an agent blocked awaiting user confirmation in a window the operator is not watching. The condition is invisible to the operator and unbounded in duration.

Crew Chief surfaces every running session on the bar, escalating the indicator when a session requires input or has completed. The panel enumerates sessions by project, harness, state and age, ordered by attention required.

Adapters are provided for Claude Code and Codex, with a single command reporter allowing any other harness to register. The widget operates locally with no network access, and carries 23 offline tests.

#AI #Agents #DeveloperTools #Omarchy #OpenSource
targets.posting_note: Crew Chief has 8 copies on 66 views, a 12 percent conversion, the second best in the set behind Bazaar. It is under-viewed rather than under-converting, so this one is worth pushing hardest on reach.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: the widget template (the one that matters most)
targets.angle: Not a widget. Sells the security architecture and the gate lane. This is the fork-and-credit asset.
targets.x_post:
every plugin in the omarchy marketplace is somebody's first quickshell code. mine included. i shipped defects i then had to sweep back out.

so i open sourced the sweep, encoded. an omarchy widget template with nine pre-submit gates, a node testable parse layer so you can unit test a qml widget with no compositor running, and six qml security rules that each map to a real bug that reached a real listing.

gh repo create --template and you start from a tree that already passes.

MIT. if you are building for omarchy quattro on hyprland, start here instead of from scratch.

#Omarchy #Hyprland #Quickshell #OpenSource
targets.li_personal:
The most useful thing I have published for Omarchy is not a plugin.

Every plugin in that marketplace, which crossed 1,300 listings this month, is somebody's first Quickshell code. Mine were too, and I shipped defects I later had to go back and sweep out of shipped entries. A reviewer found a server side request forgery hole in one of mine on submission and was right about it.

So the template is that experience written down as enforcement. Nine pre submit gates that refuse rather than warn. A parse layer that loads in Node as well as Quickshell, so the whole data path unit tests without a compositor. Six QML rules, each of which maps to a specific defect that reached a real listing: plain text rendering because AutoText sniffs strings for HTML and a hostile payload can make a desktop widget fetch a remote image, bounded curl arguments because an unbounded body freezes the shell's UI thread inside JSON.parse, and so on.

Above that sits a submission lane with one rule: no layer may report a conclusion whose scope it never established. A gate that could not run reports unproven. Never pass, never not applicable. I wrote that rule because every layer of this stack, mine included, had at some point reported success without having checked anything.

One command to instantiate. It is MIT, and you do not owe me anything for it.

#OpenSource #Linux #Omarchy #Quickshell #SecureCoding
targets.li_company:
Intent Solutions has published the Omarchy Widget Template, the scaffold underlying every plugin in its Omarchy portfolio.

The Omarchy plugin marketplace passed 1,300 listings this month, and for most contributors a plugin is their first Quickshell project. The template encodes the security and testability patterns that shipped entries earned through defect remediation, so that a new widget begins in a state that already passes pre submission review.

It provides nine hash pinned pre submit gates covering exec injection, QML overflow, request forgery via user supplied hosts, panel window type correctness and manifest and runtime consistency; a pure data layer that loads in Node as well as in Quickshell so the parse path is testable without a running compositor; and CI wiring.

The governing rule of the submission lane is that no verification layer may report a conclusion whose scope it never established. A check that could not execute reports as unproven rather than as passing or as not applicable.

Released under the MIT licence.

#OpenSource #SecureCoding #Linux #Omarchy #EngineeringStandards
targets.posting_note: This is the post that pays back the most over time and it is the one with no marketplace counter attached, so it gets judged purely on the writing. If you can only give one of these a real push, give it this one. The SSRF admission is deliberate, do not soften it, it is what makes the rest credible.

targets.subject: Omarchy packet: the portfolio page
targets.angle: The whole body of work as one thing. Hook is the self-updating table.
targets.x_post:
put all eight of my omarchy plugins on one page, plus the widget template they are built from.

the view and copy counts in that table are generated straight from the omarchy marketplace catalog, not typed in. a readme quoting a number a human typed in july is a readme that is wrong in august, and that marketplace adds dozens of listings a day.

it also renders the one plugin that is NOT listed as not listed, with a doc explaining exactly why. hiding that row would have been easier and worse.

#Omarchy #Hyprland #ArchLinux #OpenSource
targets.li_personal:
A README that quotes a number a human typed in is a README that is already wrong.

I put the eight Omarchy plugins I have shipped on one page this week, along with the widget template they are all built from. The metrics table on it is generated: it reads the marketplace catalog and the stats endpoint at refresh time, a scheduled job reruns it daily, and the same script runs as a check on every pull request so a hand edit fails the build.

Two details in it that I would defend in a review.

The install commands are read out of the marketplace's own field rather than written by me, so the page structurally cannot print a command the listing disagrees with. And the ids come from a file in the repo rather than from the catalog, so if the marketplace ever renames or drops one of my listings, the row survives and reads not listed instead of quietly disappearing. A row that vanishes is a row nobody investigates.

That second one is not hypothetical. One of the eight is genuinely not listed right now, because a marketplace reviewer found a real security hole in it and I have not closed it yet. The page says so, and links the writeup.

#OpenSource #Linux #Omarchy #EngineeringStandards #DeveloperTools
targets.li_company:
Intent Solutions has published a consolidated portfolio page for its Omarchy desktop plugins, covering eight shipped entries and the shared widget template they derive from.

The engagement metrics on the page are generated rather than maintained. A script reads the marketplace catalog and statistics endpoints at refresh time, a scheduled job reruns it daily, and the same script executes in check mode on every pull request, so a manually edited table fails continuous integration.

Two constraints were designed in. Install commands are read from the marketplace's own catalog field rather than authored, so the page cannot present an install command that contradicts the listing. Plugin identifiers are read from a repository file rather than from the catalog, so a renamed or delisted plugin renders explicitly as not listed rather than silently disappearing from the table.

The page currently reports one entry as not listed, with a linked document stating the unresolved security finding responsible and the remediation required to close it.

#OpenSource #EngineeringStandards #Linux #Omarchy #DeveloperTools
targets.posting_note: Post this one last in the sequence, after at least three of the individual plugins have gone out. It reads as a summary, and a summary lands better once people have seen a couple of the parts.
